lessons.title: Once a day, from the motion works
explanation: Motion works turn the hour wheel twice a day. A date-driving wheel takes that motion down to one turn in twenty-four hours. A finger on that driver then pushes a 31-tooth date disc one step, usually around midnight.

Force the disc while that finger still sits in a tooth and the jumper is half-cocked. The finger bends, a tooth chips, or the setting clutch slips. Changeover is a loaded mesh, not a free wheel you can spin from the crown.
lessons.example: At 23:40 the finger is already in a date-disc gap. Turning the crown in the date position fights that finger. The disc cannot jump, so the finger or a tooth yields.
lessons.whyItMatters: A simple date is a once-a-day push from the motion works. Treat it as a free spinner and you jam the changeover.

quiz.stem: What actually advances a simple date disc once each day?
quiz.correctAnswer: A finger on a 24-hour driver fed by the motion works

distractors.text: The balance, which trips a date pallet every 86,400 swings
distractors.rationale: The oscillator meters time. It does not push the date disc.

distractors.text: The mainspring barrel, which clicks the disc each time you wind
distractors.rationale: Winding stores work. It does not index the date.

distractors.text: The seconds hand, which carries a pin that hits the disc at 60
distractors.rationale: Seconds are display. The date driver turns once a day.

quiz.correctExplanation: Hour wheel, 24-hour driver, finger, 31-tooth disc. That is the simple date.
objectiveIds: Advance a date disc once a day from the motion works

quiz.stem: The date-driving wheel in this simple calendar turns:
quiz.correctAnswer: Once per day, so its finger can push one tooth of a 31-tooth disc

distractors.text: Once per hour, matching the minute hand as a date stepper
distractors.rationale: An hourly stepper would burn through the month in a day.

distractors.text: Once per week, because seven is the natural calendar ratio
distractors.rationale: A week wheel is a different extra. Simple date is daily.

distractors.text: With every balance swing, which is how a disc stays in step
distractors.rationale: The timebase does not index the disc. The motion works do.

quiz.correctExplanation: One turn a day, one tooth, 31 days around the disc.
objectiveIds: Advance a date disc once a day from the motion works

quiz.stem: You force the date from the crown at 23:40. The likely result is:
quiz.correctAnswer: A jammed finger or chipped tooth, because the changeover is already loaded

distractors.text: A cleaner jump, because load at midnight is how dates are meant to be set
distractors.rationale: Load is the hazard. Setting through it fights the finger.

distractors.text: A faster balance, because the disc stores extra impulse for the pallet
distractors.rationale: The date disc is display gearing. It does not impulse the oscillator.

distractors.text: A perpetual month, because forcing the disc teaches it February
distractors.rationale: Force does not add a month cam. It bends steel.

quiz.correctExplanation: Finger already in the gap, jumper half-cocked. Pushing then yields a part.
objectiveIds: Predict a jammed setting if you force the date near the changeover

lessons.title: Thirty-one teeth and a midnight finger
explanation: Hour wheel to date driver to a 31-tooth disc is the whole simple date. The driver turns once per day. Its finger or cam advances one tooth, and a jumper spring parks the disc on a number until the next midnight.

Slow dates drag that finger across a tooth for hours. Instant dates store a spring and dump it at a trip. Either way the mesh is loaded near the jump. Setting through that window fights the finger with the stem.

Predict the jam: crown in the date position, time showing late evening into the first hour, and you push. The finger is already in the gap. The disc cannot jump, so something yields — usually the finger, a tooth, or a clutched pinion.
lessons.example: A student sets the date at 23:50 on a slow-change calibre. The finger is deep in a tooth. The crown fights, the finger bends, and the disc later hangs between two numbers.
lessons.whyItMatters: Know which wheel pushes the disc, and when that push is live, or date-setting becomes a way to break the motion works.

quiz.stem: How does a simple date disc differ from the going train in this machine?
quiz.correctAnswer: The disc is display advanced once a day; the going train still counts the unwind

distractors.text: The disc meters the second; the going train only prints the date
distractors.rationale: The oscillator meters. The date disc is a daily display.

distractors.text: The disc stores the mainspring; the going train is only a jumper
distractors.rationale: Stored work is still the spring in the barrel.

distractors.text: They are two names for the same 31-tooth escape wheel
distractors.rationale: Escape wheel and date disc are different jobs.

quiz.correctExplanation: Motion works, 24-hour driver, finger, disc. The timebase is not in that chain.
objectiveIds: Advance a date disc once a day from the motion works

quiz.stem: Trace a simple date from the cannon pinion to a new number on the disc. After the hour wheel comes:
quiz.correctAnswer: A 24-hour driver whose finger then pushes one tooth of the 31-tooth disc

distractors.text: The escape wheel, whose pallet then prints the date on the jumper
distractors.rationale: The escapement meters the going train. It does not index the disc.

distractors.text: The barrel arbor, which clicks the disc each time you wind the crown
distractors.rationale: Winding is a different path. Date comes from the motion works.

distractors.text: The fourth wheel, treated here as a 31-tooth calendar driver
distractors.rationale: The fourth wheel is seconds of the going train, not a date driver.

quiz.correctExplanation: Cannon, hour wheel, 24-hour driver, finger, disc. That is the path.
objectiveIds: Advance a date disc once a day from the motion works

quiz.stem: A slow date is mid-jump at 23:45 and you set from the crown. Predict the failure:
quiz.correctAnswer: The loaded finger or a tooth yields, and the disc can hang between numbers

distractors.text: The jump finishes cleaner, because stem torque is the intended midnight spring
distractors.rationale: Stem torque fights the finger. It is not the date spring.

distractors.text: The balance gains amplitude, which is how dates are supposed to be oiled
distractors.rationale: Setting the disc does not oil or feed the oscillator.

distractors.text: The month cam advances, so a simple date becomes an annual calendar
distractors.rationale: A simple date has no month cam. Force does not add one.

quiz.correctExplanation: Changeover is a loaded mesh. Forcing it bends the finger or chips a tooth.
objectiveIds: Predict a jammed setting if you force the date near the changeover

lessons.title: What the month cam has to remember
explanation: Remembering is the cost. A simple date has a 31-tooth disc and a human. After a 30-day month, and after February, someone must skip the extra numbers. The mechanism does not know the month.

Annual calendars add a 12-month cam or program wheel that withholds the 31st on short months. February is still a lie: the cam treats it as 30, so a human still corrects once a year, usually on March 1.

Perpetual calendars add a four-year, often 48-month, program that includes February 29. Mechanism cost is extra cams, extra fingers, extra jumpers. A human still appears if the watch stops for days, or in Gregorian exceptions such as 2100.
lessons.example: On 1 March a simple date still shows 29 or 30 from February. An annual needs the wearer then. A running perpetual has already skipped to 1 March, because its program wheel included the leap day.
lessons.whyItMatters: Simple, annual, and perpetual are not grades of a watch. They are three answers to how many month lengths the mechanism stores.

quiz.stem: How do simple, annual, and perpetual calendars differ in what they remember?
quiz.correctAnswer: Simple remembers 31 days; annual remembers 30 versus 31; perpetual also remembers leap Februaries

distractors.text: Simple remembers leap years; annual remembers only hours; perpetual remembers nothing
distractors.rationale: Simple remembers the least. Perpetual remembers the most.

distractors.text: They differ only by how many jewels sit under the date disc
distractors.rationale: Jewel count is not a month program.

distractors.text: Annual and perpetual are two names for the same 31-tooth disc
distractors.rationale: A 31-tooth disc is the simple date. The others add cams.

quiz.correctExplanation: The extra cams are extra memory. Cost tracks what the mechanism stores.
objectiveIds: Distinguish simple, annual, and perpetual calendars by what they remember

quiz.stem: Which calendar still needs a human every February in a non-leap year?
quiz.correctAnswer: Simple and annual; a running perpetual has a program for that February

distractors.text: Only the perpetual, because leap cams always jam in February
distractors.rationale: The perpetual is the one built to pass February without a hand.

distractors.text: None of them, because a 31-tooth disc already knows the month length
distractors.rationale: A 31-tooth disc does not know February. That is the simple date's gap.

distractors.text: Only world-time watches, because cities encode the calendar
distractors.rationale: Cities are a time-zone display. They do not store month lengths.

quiz.correctExplanation: Annual treats February as 30. Simple treats every month as 31. Both need a hand in February.
objectiveIds: Predict which one needs a human in February

quiz.stem: An annual calendar and a perpetual calendar on 1 March of a leap year. Who needed a wearer overnight?
quiz.correctAnswer: The annual, whose month cam still treated February as thirty days

distractors.text: The perpetual, whose four-year wheel always stops on 29 February
distractors.rationale: The perpetual's program includes the leap day. The annual's does not.

distractors.text: Neither, because both discs are 31-tooth and therefore leap-aware
distractors.rationale: Tooth count on the date disc does not encode leap years.

distractors.text: Both, because only a tourbillon cage can remember February
distractors.rationale: A cage averages a positional error. It is not a month program.

quiz.correctExplanation: Annual remembers short months except the leap rule. Perpetual stores that rule in a four-year program.
objectiveIds: Predict which one needs a human in February

lessons.title: Fifty-nine teeth against the sky
explanation: Two moons painted on a disc, 59 teeth around the edge, one tooth per day: that is the common moonphase. The disc turns once in 59 days, so each moon takes 29.5 days to cross the aperture. The sky's synodic month is about 29.53 days.

Drive comes from a reduction off the date or hour path, not from the oscillator. A star wheel or finger advances the 59-tooth wheel once a day, the same daily cadence as a simple date, geared for a slower disc.

The 0.03-day gap per lunation is accepted on purpose. It builds to about a day of error in two and a half years. A finer tooth count shrinks that gap. It does not make the disc a telescope; it is still a ratio.
lessons.example: A 59-tooth disc set at a true full moon is about eleven hours late after one year of daily steps. After roughly 2.7 years the aperture is a day off the sky, and you recorrect the disc.
lessons.whyItMatters: Moonphase is a gear ratio with a known residual, not a picture that tracks the sky by magic.

quiz.stem: How is a common moon disc driven so that it approximates a lunation?
quiz.correctAnswer: A daily finger advances a 59-tooth disc that carries two moons

distractors.text: The balance trips a moon pallet once per swing so the disc tracks the sky
distractors.rationale: The oscillator does not index the moon. A daily reduction does.

distractors.text: The rotor winds a separate moon barrel that turns with the wearer
distractors.rationale: Automatic winding is a different extra. Moonphase is a ratio.

distractors.text: A 31-tooth date disc is the lunation, read through a second aperture
distractors.rationale: 31 days is a month of dates, not a synodic month of 29.5 days.

quiz.correctExplanation: 59 teeth, two moons, one step a day. Each painted moon takes 29.5 days to pass.
objectiveIds: Drive a moon disc from a reduction that approximates the lunation

quiz.stem: A 59-tooth moon disc with two moons accepts, on purpose, which error?
quiz.correctAnswer: About 0.03 days per lunation, building to a day in roughly 2.7 years

distractors.text: Exactly zero, because 59 is the sky's true tooth count
distractors.rationale: The synodic month is 29.53 days, not 29.5. The gap is the point.

distractors.text: One hour per day, which is why the disc must be reset every night
distractors.rationale: The disc is stepped once a day. The residual is minutes per month, not an hour a day.

distractors.text: A full month per year, which is the perpetual calendar's moon error
distractors.rationale: Calendars store month lengths. This error is a lunation ratio.

quiz.correctExplanation: 29.5 versus 29.53 days. That residual is the 59-tooth compromise.
objectiveIds: State the error a 59-tooth disc accepts on purpose

quiz.stem: After two and a half years a 59-tooth moon disc that was set true will typically:
quiz.correctAnswer: Sit about a day off the sky, which is the residual the ratio accepted

distractors.text: Stay exact, because two moons cancel the 0.03-day gap
distractors.rationale: Two moons give 29.5 days each. They do not cancel the 0.03.

distractors.text: Lock the date jumper, which is how moonphase corrects February
distractors.rationale: Moonphase is not a month program. It does not run the calendar.

distractors.text: Gain a full hour, because the fourth wheel drives the moon disc
distractors.rationale: The fourth wheel is going-train seconds. Moonphase is a daily reduction.

quiz.correctExplanation: The accepted gap accumulates. Recorrect the disc; do not blame the timebase.
objectiveIds: State the error a 59-tooth disc accepts on purpose

lessons.title: Second hour hand, or a city disc
explanation: Local hours still come from the motion works. A true GMT adds a 24-hour hand on its own wheel, settable without dragging those local hours — or the other way around: local hours jump while the 24-hour hand holds home time.

World time is a different display. A disc of cities sits against a 24-hour ring. You index one city to local time; every other city reads off the same ring. No independent 24-hour hand is required for that reading.
A 24-hour hand locked to local hours is neither. It only restates the same count on a 24-hour scale. Independent set is the GMT test. A city ring is the world-time test. Do not swap those names.
lessons.example: You land and jump local hours with the crown. A true GMT 24-hour hand still shows home time. A world-time disc instead lets you rotate a city to the new local hour and read the others on the ring.
lessons.whyItMatters: GMT and world time are two mechanisms. Calling both 'a second time zone' hides which wheel you can actually set.

quiz.stem: What makes a 24-hour hand a true GMT rather than a locked extra hour?
quiz.correctAnswer: It can be set independently of the local-hour motion works

distractors.text: It is painted 24 hours, even if it is geared 1:1 to local hours
distractors.rationale: A locked 24-hour hand only restates local time on another scale.

distractors.text: It sits on the chronograph runner and starts when you push
distractors.rationale: A chronograph is a stopwatch register, not a second time zone.

distractors.text: It shares a cannon pinion, so setting hours must drag it
distractors.rationale: Independent set is the test. Dragging it with local hours fails that test.

quiz.correctExplanation: Independent 24-hour set, or jumping local hours while the 24-hour hand holds. That is GMT.
objectiveIds: Add a 24-hour hand that can be set independently of local time

quiz.stem: You need home time to stay put while local hours jump after a flight. The mechanism that does that is:
quiz.correctAnswer: A 24-hour GMT hand on its own wheel, left alone while local hours index

distractors.text: A city disc with no independent hand, read as if it were home time
distractors.rationale: A city disc is world time. It does not hold a second independently set hour.

distractors.text: A date finger, jumped twelve times to stand in for a 24-hour hand
distractors.rationale: The date disc is a daily display. It is not a second hour hand.

distractors.text: A locked 24-hour hand geared to the local hour wheel at 2:1
distractors.rationale: Geared 2:1 to local hours, it jumps when local hours jump.

quiz.correctExplanation: Local hours index. The 24-hour wheel stays. That independent set is the GMT.
objectiveIds: Add a 24-hour hand that can be set independently of local time

quiz.stem: How does a world-time city disc differ from a true GMT 24-hour hand?
quiz.correctAnswer: The disc shows many cities on one ring; GMT is one independently settable 24-hour hand

distractors.text: They are the same wheel with two names, both locked to local hours
distractors.rationale: City disc and independent 24-hour hand are different displays.

distractors.text: World time is the date disc; GMT is the moon disc read as hours
distractors.rationale: Date and moon are other extras. Neither is a time-zone display.

distractors.text: A city disc can be set only at midnight, like a date changeover
distractors.rationale: World time is indexed by rotating a ring, not by a midnight finger.

quiz.correctExplanation: Cities on a ring versus one 24-hour hand you can set without dragging local time.
objectiveIds: Distinguish a true GMT from a world-time disc that only shows cities

lessons.title: Noise from a second release
explanation: Strike needs stored work. A second barrel, or a second release of a dedicated spring, powers a hammer that hits a gong or the case. The going mainspring keeps its job: feeding the timebase.

Release is a coincidence. An alarm disc or snail is set to the chosen hour. When the hour wheel's catch matches that disc, a lever frees the hammer train. The noise is that train running down, not the going train ringing.

Dumping the going barrel into a hammer would sag amplitude and pull the rate. Keep the strike on its own spring, or on a release that cannot empty the going barrel. The timebase should not notice the bell.
lessons.example: A two-barrel alarm: you wind one crown for time, another for the hammer spring. At the set hour a lever drops, the hammer train runs, the case rings, and the going train's swing stays in its usual band.
lessons.whyItMatters: An alarm is a second store and a second release. Share the going spring and you buy a rate error with the noise.

quiz.stem: Where should the work for an alarm hammer be stored in this lesson's machine?
quiz.correctAnswer: In a second spring or a second release that does not empty the going barrel

distractors.text: In the going mainspring, dumped into the hammer at the set hour
distractors.rationale: Dumping the going barrel sags the timebase. That is the failure.

distractors.text: In the date jumper, which is already a spring that clicks once a day
distractors.rationale: A date jumper parks a disc. It does not run a hammer train.

distractors.text: In the hairspring, whose extra coils are what make the case ring
distractors.rationale: The hairspring is the timebase. Noise is a hammer train.

quiz.correctExplanation: Second barrel or dedicated release. The going spring still feeds the oscillator.
objectiveIds: Store a second spring or a second release so a hammer can strike

quiz.stem: If the alarm empties the going barrel into the hammer, the rate typically:
quiz.correctAnswer: Sags because amplitude falls while the timebase is starved of torque

distractors.text: Improves, because a ringing case is a more isochronous oscillator
distractors.rationale: The case is not the oscillator. Starving the balance hurts the rate.

distractors.text: Holds, because hammers always take power from the cannon pinion only
distractors.rationale: The cannon pinion is display. A shared barrel is the going train.

distractors.text: Gains exactly an hour, which is the alarm's natural compensation
distractors.rationale: There is no hour of compensation. There is a missing torque.

quiz.correctExplanation: Strike load on the going spring steals swing. Keep the hammer off that barrel.
objectiveIds: Predict what the alarm must not do to the going train's rate

quiz.stem: The watch rings and the seconds hand then crawls. The first suspect is:
quiz.correctAnswer: The hammer train stole torque from the going barrel instead of a second spring

distractors.text: A city disc that became the timebase when the alarm released
distractors.rationale: World time is a display. It does not ring or starve the barrel.

distractors.text: A date finger that always rings the case at midnight as designed
distractors.rationale: A date finger pushes a disc. A crawling seconds hand is a starved train.

distractors.text: A 59-tooth moon disc, whose residual always shows up as a slow hand
distractors.rationale: Moonphase error is a display offset, not a drop in amplitude.

quiz.correctExplanation: Noise plus a crawling train means the strike shared the going spring.
objectiveIds: Predict what the alarm must not do to the going train's rate

lessons.title: Rotor motion that must not overwind
explanation: Oscillating mass on the wearer's motion turns a reduction into the ratchet wheel of the barrel. That is automatic winding: the crown is no longer the only path that stores work in the mainspring.

A reversing gear, a pair of pawls, or a wobble pinion decides whether both directions count. A click still stops the barrel from unwinding back through that train. Without the click, the rotor would become an unwind path.

Overwind is the other failure. A slipping bridle on the outer coil lets the fully wound spring slide on the barrel wall. Trace that bridle, or a stop-work if fitted, as the safety. The rotor may keep turning. The spring must not be forced past its set.
lessons.example: Rotor left, reverser A drives the ratchet; rotor right, reverser B takes over. At full wind the bridle slips on the barrel wall with a faint click, and amplitude no longer climbs.
lessons.whyItMatters: Automatic winding is a path from a mass to the ratchet, plus a bridle so that path cannot wreck the spring.

quiz.stem: Trace automatic winding from the wearer's motion to a charged mainspring. After the rotor comes:
quiz.correctAnswer: A reduction into the ratchet, with a click so the barrel cannot unwind that way

distractors.text: The escape wheel, which the rotor impulses instead of the pallet
distractors.rationale: The rotor winds the barrel. It does not replace the escapement.

distractors.text: The date finger, which stores work in the 31-tooth disc
distractors.rationale: The date disc is display. Stored work is still the mainspring.

distractors.text: The cannon pinion, which the rotor turns to wind the hands
distractors.rationale: Hands display a count. Winding charges the barrel, not the hands.

quiz.correctExplanation: Rotor, reduction, ratchet, barrel. Click against unwind. Bridle against overwind.
objectiveIds: Convert a rotor's motion into winding without letting the spring overwind

quiz.stem: The safety that stops an automatic from overwinding the mainspring is typically:
quiz.correctAnswer: A slipping bridle on the outer coil, or a stop-work if the calibre uses one

distractors.text: The hairspring, which locks the rotor once amplitude looks high enough
distractors.rationale: The hairspring meters the balance. It does not cap the barrel.

distractors.text: The date jumper, which slips so the rotor cannot turn at night
distractors.rationale: A jumper parks a disc. Overwind safety sits in the barrel.

distractors.text: Removing the click so extra turns can dump back through the rotor
distractors.rationale: Losing the click is an unwind path, not a bridle.

quiz.correctExplanation: Bridle slips on the barrel wall at full wind. The rotor may still turn.
objectiveIds: Trace a reversing gear or a slipping bridle as the safety

quiz.stem: If the bridle seizes on the barrel wall and the rotor keeps turning, predict the failure:
quiz.correctAnswer: The spring is forced past its set, coils distort, and later torque becomes uneven

distractors.text: The watch becomes a perpetual calendar, because extra turns store February
distractors.rationale: Overwind does not add a month program. It stresses the spring.

distractors.text: Amplitude falls to zero at once, which is how bridles are supposed to protect
distractors.rationale: A seized bridle fails to slip. Protection is the slip, not a stop of the oscillator.

distractors.text: The cannon pinion unscrews, which is the usual overwind fuse
distractors.rationale: Overwind is a barrel problem. The cannon pinion is display.

quiz.correctExplanation: No slip, continued rotor, forced set. The bridle was the safety and it seized.
objectiveIds: Convert a rotor's motion into winding without letting the spring overwind

lessons.title: The mass that turns with the wrist
explanation: Wearer's motion is the input. The rotor is the mass that turns on a bearing — ball, jewel, or both — so that motion becomes a rotation the winding train can use. Without that mass, the reversing gears have nothing to rectify.

Unidirectional winding uses a pawl or a single reverser: one direction drives the ratchet, the other freewheels. Bidirectional winding uses two reversers, a pair of pawls, or a wobble pinion so both directions drive.

Read the reverser, not the advertisement. If only one path meshes, half the rotor's travel is discarded. If both paths mesh, both directions count. A seized reverser that never freewheels will drag and steal from the going train.
lessons.example: A magic-lever or two-reverser stack: rotor clockwise drives wheel A, counterclockwise drives wheel B, both turn the ratchet the same way. A one-pawl rotor clicks on the return and adds no wind.
lessons.whyItMatters: The rotor is a mass. Unidirectional versus bidirectional is a fact about the reverser, not about how heavy the weight looks.

quiz.stem: In this lesson, the rotor is which part of automatic winding?
quiz.correctAnswer: The mass that turns with the wearer's motion so the winding train has an input

distractors.text: The slipping bridle, renamed rotor because it lives in the barrel
distractors.rationale: The bridle is overwind safety. The rotor is the oscillating mass.

distractors.text: The hairspring, whose coils are what the wrist is supposed to wind
distractors.rationale: The hairspring belongs to the timebase. The rotor winds the barrel.

distractors.text: The 24-hour GMT hand, which stores work as it turns with local hours
distractors.rationale: A GMT hand is a display. It does not wind the mainspring.

quiz.correctExplanation: Mass on a bearing, turned by the wrist. That rotation is the winding input.
objectiveIds: Name the rotor as the mass that turns with the wearer's motion

quiz.stem: You watch the rotor reverse and the ratchet still advances. That predicts:
quiz.correctAnswer: Bidirectional winding: a reverser or second pawl is making the return count

distractors.text: Unidirectional winding, because a ratchet that always turns means the return is freewheeling
distractors.rationale: Freewheel means the ratchet does not advance on the return.

distractors.text: A seized bridle, which is how rotors are supposed to stop the going train
distractors.rationale: A bridle sits in the barrel. Reversers sit in the winding train.

distractors.text: A world-time disc, whose cities wind the spring as they rotate
distractors.rationale: A city disc is a time-zone display. It does not wind.

quiz.correctExplanation: Both directions drive the ratchet. That is bidirectional, read from the reverser.
objectiveIds: Predict unidirectional versus bidirectional winding from the reverser

quiz.stem: How does a unidirectional rotor differ from a bidirectional one at the reverser?
quiz.correctAnswer: Unidirectional freewheels one way; bidirectional has a path that drives both ways

distractors.text: Unidirectional is always a heavier mass; bidirectional is a lighter disc
distractors.rationale: Mass is not the sequencer. The reverser is.

distractors.text: They are identical; only the date jumper decides which way counts
distractors.rationale: The date jumper parks a disc. It does not rectify the rotor.

distractors.text: Bidirectional freewheels both ways, which is why it cannot overwind
distractors.rationale: Freewheeling both ways would wind nothing. Overwind safety is the bridle.

quiz.correctExplanation: Count the driving paths. One path is unidirectional. Two is bidirectional.
objectiveIds: Predict unidirectional versus bidirectional winding from the reverser

lessons.title: Reserve as a barrel reading
explanation: Barrel state is what the hand reports. Remaining turns of the spring are not a second, and they are not the timebase. A power-reserve indicator is a display of how far the barrel arbor and the barrel drum have moved relative to each other.

Two common converters: a differential that subtracts drum rotation from arbor rotation and sends the difference to a hand, or a cone or snail on the arbor whose feeler turns that height into an angle on the dial.

Keep that gearing off the escape. Steal from the timebase and you have bought a rate error in order to print a number. The indicator may drag a little torque from the barrel. It must not meter the unwind.
lessons.example: Wind the crown: the reserve hand climbs as the arbor turns inside a still drum. Let the watch run: the drum unwinds, the differential walks the other way, and the hand falls, while the balance still owns the second.
lessons.whyItMatters: Reserve is a barrel reading. Treat it as a second timebase and you will chase the indicator when the oscillator was never involved.

quiz.stem: A power-reserve hand is supposed to indicate remaining spring by:
quiz.correctAnswer: Reading arbor-versus-drum motion, without becoming a second timebase

distractors.text: Counting balance swings and printing that count as hours of reserve
distractors.rationale: Swings are the timebase. Reserve is barrel state.

distractors.text: Coupling a chronograph runner until the spring looks empty
distractors.rationale: A chronograph is a stopwatch register, not a barrel reading.

distractors.text: Advancing the 31-tooth date disc once per remaining hour
distractors.rationale: The date disc is a daily display. It does not track the barrel.

quiz.correctExplanation: Arbor and drum. Difference to a hand. The oscillator is not in that chain.
objectiveIds: Indicate remaining spring without stealing the timebase

quiz.stem: Trace reserve from a wound barrel to a climbing hand. The converter is typically:
quiz.correctAnswer: A differential of arbor versus drum, or a cone or snail a feeler follows

distractors.text: The pallet fork, which prints reserve as it locks each escape tooth
distractors.rationale: The pallet belongs to the timebase. Reserve is a barrel display.

distractors.text: The city disc, rotated until the remaining hours match a town
distractors.rationale: World time is a zone display. It does not read the spring.

distractors.text: The cannon pinion, which is already a count of remaining turns
distractors.rationale: The cannon pinion carries the minute hand. It does not subtract drum from arbor.

quiz.correctExplanation: Differential or cone. Either turns remaining spring into an angle on the dial.
objectiveIds: Trace the differential or cone that turns reserve into a hand

quiz.stem: How should a reserve indicator differ from the going train's timebase?
quiz.correctAnswer: It reports barrel state; it must not meter the unwind or load the escape

distractors.text: It is the timebase; the balance is only a spare if the hand stops
distractors.rationale: The oscillator meters. The reserve hand is a barrel reading.

distractors.text: It must be geared to the fourth wheel so seconds and reserve stay locked
distractors.rationale: Locking reserve to the fourth wheel would steal from the timebase.

distractors.text: It replaces the slipping bridle, so a climbing hand is overwind safety
distractors.rationale: The bridle is still the overwind safety. The hand only reports.

quiz.correctExplanation: Display of remaining turns. Keep it off the escape.
objectiveIds: Indicate remaining spring without stealing the timebase
